pages.disposition: Article title, author and collection background. The author visited Dhekenal in 1854, Hindole in the following year, and near Bhapore shortly before writing. General population/place names and references to Piddington, Sterling and Mills are context, not additional glossed Juang forms.

Self-name Juanga is ingested. Puttooa, glossed by the author as quasi “the people of the leaf”, is expressly the neighbours’ name, not attributed to Juang speech; preserve as an excluded non-target control. Names of leaves sál, jamoon, koorye, chaldua, bur, peepul, mhowa and kendooa occur in English ethnographic prose without Juang-language attribution or lexical glosses and are context only.

Dress legend, ornaments and English ethnographic narrative. Thakoorani, Seeta and Rishi occur in English narrative without source attribution as Juang expressions or direct glosses. No fabricated Juang counterpart is extracted.
Dance, history and village description, with English narrative and geographic names only. No additional explicitly attested Juang lexical unit.

Pudhan title is ingested with exact attribution. Moolee Pudhan and Kumlee are persons named in the narrative, not additional glossed common-word entries. Toonga, kurka and panee aloo are explicitly names supplied by “our Ooriya attendants” and are excluded non-target controls. Mhowa is an unglossed plant term in English narrative. Hunting/cultivation/religion context provides no further Juang utterances.

Free English prayer “Lord, let the bears and the tigers flee when they see us. Let them not meet us.” has no Juang original printed, so is preserved as context only. Bysakh is a month name in English narrative, not a Juang lexical response. Marriage narrative and named people supply no additional glossed Juang units.

Samuells explicitly states that he collected the list of words and phrases. His language-affiliation suggestions and comparison of dress with Coorumbas, Chenchoos and Holiers are attributed historical commentary only; no relatedness edges are inferred. The quoted extract from Pharoah’s Gazetteer p.516 concerns dress, with no target lexical form.
End of comparative ethnographic discussion followed by 24 aligned English/Juanga vocabulary cells. All ingested; alternatives remain source variants, and full responses remain whole.

Seven further aligned vocabulary cells, all ingested. The separator then begins Dr. A. Sprenger’s separate article “On the origin and progress of writing down historical facts among the Musalmans”, outside this source.

scope_decisions: All whole responses retained, including inflected and multiword expressions. No stems are inferred. No phonetic key is supplied in the article; accents and vowel doubling remain literal. Historical affiliations and neighbouring-language terms are not converted into donor or cognate edges.
edition: Printed title and running heads date 1856; retain source year1856 despite BHL catalogue1857.
native: No native-script word list or counterpart is printed.
method: Manual original-image reading of all nine article pages and three interleaved plates; no OCR used in this recovery.
